runs.t: Red Hat Enterprise Linux System Administration I | Study file
This chapter teaches you how Linux starts and manages its background programs with systemd. You learn to list services, check their state, and start, stop, restart, mask and enable them with
Topics in this chapter, in book order:
systemd is the first program Linux starts, and it starts and manages all the services after it.

Think of a building manager. When the building opens, the manager switches on the lights, heating and lifts. Later the manager can switch on other things when someone needs them. systemd does this for Linux, at boot time and on a running system.
are processes that wait or run in the background doing tasks. They usually start at boot and run until shutdown or until someone stops them. Many daemon names end in the letter
, in the systemd sense, often means one or more daemons. But starting a service can also make a one-time change and leave no daemon running afterward. That type is called
systemd has PID 1 on RHEL. Its features include: starting many services at the same time (faster boot); starting daemons on demand; managing
(a network service waits for the network); and tracking related processes together with Linux control groups.
Boot  ->  systemd (PID 1)  ->  starts atd, auditd, chronyd, crond ...

PID 1 is the first process (see Chapter 8).
systemd is PID 1. It starts services at boot and on demand.
systemd manages things called units, and the three common kinds are service, socket and path units.
Think of three kinds of staff. One always works at the front desk. One waits at the door until a visitor rings. One waits until a parcel arrives.
. It represents a system service, and is used to start often-used daemons such as a web server.

is a doorway that programs use to talk to each other. If a client connects to it, systemd starts the daemon and hands over the connection. This delays a start at boot and starts rarely used services on demand.
. It waits until a file system change happens, then starts a service. It is common for services that use spool directories (folders where jobs wait), such as printing.
name.service  ->  a daemon, such as a web server
name.socket   ->  systemd waits for a client to connect, then starts the daemon
name.path     ->  systemd waits for a file change, then starts the service

Restart stops and starts a service; reload makes it re-read its configuration without stopping.
Think of a shop. A restart closes the shop and opens it again. A reload tells the shop to read its new rules while staying open.
On a restart, the process ID changes, because a new process starts. On a reload, the process ID stays the same.
Not every service can reload. If you are not sure, use
. It reloads if it can, and restarts if it cannot.

Reload keeps the same process; restart makes a new one.
Some services need other units, so stopping one service may leave it able to start again through another unit.
Think of a team. If a service needs others first, systemd starts them as needed. Some units start only on demand.
The book's example: if the CUPS print service is not running and a file is put in the print spool folder, systemd starts CUPS-related programs to do the job.

A service may also start through a socket or path unit, so stop all three to stop it fully.
Masking a service makes it impossible to start, so conflicting services cannot be started by mistake.
Think of locking a cupboard so nobody opens it by accident. Two installed services may conflict. For example, postfix and sendmail are two ways to run a mail server.

Mask to block a service completely; unmask to allow it again.
A disabled service can be started manually or by other unit files, but it does not start automatically at boot. A masked service does not start manually or automatically.
